svg.text: COFFEE MACHINE — THE BREW STATE MACHINE
MACHINE STATE — two singletons, one field
up once the state is back
to IDLE — so no caller can
Why the GoF State pattern and not an enum here?
Because each state carries BEHAVIOUR, not just a label: IdleState knows
how to look up a beverage, flip the state and brew; DispensingState knows
how to reject. The context passes ITSELF in, so a state drives its own exit.
Both states are stateless ⇒ private ctor + shared INSTANCE is correct ✓
Contrast Blackjack, where five label-only phases justify a plain enum.
Two states is honestly borderline — say that rather than over-selling it.
● ACQUIRE the machine monitor — everything below is one critical section
setState(DispensingState) — invisible to everyone else, see ①
machine.brewOrder(latte) — THE ONLY PLACE STOCK MOVES
setState(IdleState) · RELEASE the monitor · return the Order
Notice what is NOT in this sequence: payment.
The drink is brewed and the ingredients are gone before anyone pays. processPayment
is a separate call afterwards that only asks "amount ≥ price?" and returns a boolean —
it never marks the Order paid, never refunds, never blocks the pour.
ORDER STATUS — the second state machine
All-or-nothing: consume() checks the FULL recipe before
deducting anything, so a FAILED order leaves stock untouched. ✓
OrderStatus.IN_PROGRESS exists in the enum and is never
assigned — brewing is synchronous, so nothing is ever mid-flight.
It becomes reachable the day brewOrder is handed to an executor:

g.text: PAY-THEN-POUR: THE FIX YOU SHOULD VOLUNTEER
Today: placeOrder brews immediately; processPayment is an afterthought that
compares two BigDecimals and returns a boolean nobody acts on.
The fix is a third state and one extra status: placeOrder reserves the recipe and
returns a PENDING order; the machine moves to AWAITING_PAYMENT; only a
successful processPayment triggers brewOrder. Insufficient funds or a timeout
releases the reservation and returns to IDLE.
That is also when Payment.orderId stops being decoration and starts being checked.
DON'T HOLD A LOCK ACROSS A 20-SECOND POUR
Right now brewOrder() is a map update, so holding the
machine monitor across it costs nothing.
A real grinder + pump takes tens of seconds. Blocking
every caller — including checkIngredients and the
refill technician — for that long is unacceptable.
Then: deduct stock under the lock, release it, pour
outside it, and let DISPENSING reject new orders.
READ THIS DIAGRAM AS TWO MACHINES, NOT ONE
• The MACHINE state (IDLE / DISPENSING) is about concurrency: who is allowed to call in right now.
• The ORDER status (PENDING / COMPLETED / FAILED) is about outcome: what happened to one cup.
Conflating them is the classic vending-machine mistake — you end up with a global "machine is
FAILED" state that has to be cleared by hand. Keeping them separate means one out-of-stock latte
is just a FAILED order; the machine is back to IDLE and can serve an espresso a millisecond later.
Same rule scales: per-request status vs per-resource state. Name the distinction out loud — it is
the single most transferable idea in this problem.
